subChunks.title: Online Analytical Processing vs Online Transaction Processing
subChunks.hookHtml: A query that aggregates 5 years of orders across 10 columns runs well in a warehouse but kills a transactional database. Understanding the OLAP/OLTP split drives the most important architectural decisions in data engineering.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
OLTP — Online Transaction Processing

Optimised for high-frequency, low-latency row-level operations: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT by primary key. Examples: the Academy's live apprentice database, e-commerce orders, banking transactions.

  • Many concurrent short transactions
  • Row-oriented storage (good for returning full rows)
  • Normalised schema (minimise write amplification)
  • Small result sets per query

OLAP — Online Analytical Processing

Optimised for complex analytical queries over large datasets: aggregations, GROUP BY, window functions, cross-dimensional analysis. Examples: business intelligence, data warehouses, usage analytics.

  • Few, long-running queries
  • Column-oriented storage (read only the needed columns)
  • Denormalised schema (joins are expensive at billion-row scale)
  • Large result sets, heavy aggregation

Row vs column storage

-- Row storage: each row is stored together
-- Good for: SELECT * WHERE id = 1 (one row fetch)
-- Bad for: SELECT SUM(xp) FROM apprentices (reads all columns to find xp)

-- Column storage: each column is stored together
-- Good for: SELECT SUM(xp) — reads only xp column, ignoring name/rank/etc.
-- Bad for: SELECT * WHERE id = 1 — must read from many column stores

Separation patterns

  • ETL to a data warehouse — extract from OLTP, transform, load into a columnar warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, DuckDB)
  • Read replicas for analytics — run heavy analytics on a replica to avoid impacting the primary
  • PostgreSQL HTAP — Timescale, Citus can extend PostgreSQL for analytical workloads while maintaining ACID transactions

storyBeats.text: A 'simple report' query is taking 4 minutes and crashing the production API. It is scanning the entire transactions table.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: OLTP and OLAP are different shapes of work. Row storage is efficient for transactional row-level access. Column storage is efficient for scanning millions of values in one column. Run analytics on a warehouse, not on the live operational database. The report can wait an hour for yesterday's data — the API cannot wait 4 minutes to save a transaction.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 OLAP/OLTP classification

Classify each query as OLTP or OLAP and explain why:

  1. SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 123456
  2. SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM order_items WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY revenue DESC
  3. UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100 WHERE id = 7
  4. SELECT cohort_month, AVG(days_to_first_purchase) FROM (... complex 6-table join ...) GROUP BY cohort_month
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. OLTP — primary key lookup returning one row. Fast, selective, typical transactional pattern. Should be sub-millisecond with an index on id.

2. OLAP — aggregating all order_items for the current year, grouped by product. Reads many rows and many columns. On a large table this is a heavy scan. Better run on a replica or warehouse.

3. OLTP — single row UPDATE by primary key. Highly selective write. Typical transactional operation.

4. OLAP — multi-table join producing aggregated analytics. Low frequency, high cost. This is exactly what a data warehouse or an analytics replica is for. Running this on the production OLTP database risks starving other queries of CPU and I/O.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Describe the ETL pipeline pattern for separating OLTP and OLAP workloads, including what ETL stands for and how often each step should run for a daily business report.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
ETL: Extract, Transform, Load.

Extract: Read recent changes from the OLTP database (using CDC, a timestamp-based query, or logical replication).

Transform: Clean, join, aggregate, and reshape data for analytics. Denormalise where needed for the warehouse schema (e.g. flatten orders + order_items into a wide orders_fact table).

Load: Write the prepared data into the analytical store (data warehouse or read-optimised database).

For a daily business report:
- Extract: run nightly (e.g. 2am) to copy previous day's data
- Transform: apply data quality checks, calculate derived metrics, build dimension tables
- Load: write to BigQuery/Snowflake/DuckDB — the report reads from here at 8am when the business day starts
- Frequency: daily for business reports. For real-time dashboards: streaming ETL (Kafka + Flink) or micro-batch every 5 minutes.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between row-oriented and column-oriented storage. Why is column storage better for analytical aggregations?

questions.prompt: What is the key characteristic of OLAP workloads vs OLTP?
options: OLAP involves few, complex queries aggregating large datasets; OLTP involves many, short transactions on individual rows
OLAP is always faster than OLTP
OLTP uses more tables than OLAP
OLAP requires no indexes; OLTP requires all columns indexed
questions.answer: OLAP involves few, complex queries aggregating large datasets; OLTP involves many, short transactions on individual rows
questions.explanation: OLTP: high-frequency, row-level, latency-sensitive (insert, update, select by PK). OLAP: low-frequency, high-cost, aggregate-heavy (sum, group by, window functions across millions of rows).

questions.prompt: Why is column-oriented storage faster for `SELECT SUM(revenue) FROM sales WHERE year = 2024`?
options: Only the revenue and year columns need to be read — irrelevant columns (customer_name, address, etc.) are skipped entirely
Column storage compresses data more aggressively
Column storage has fewer rows per table
Column storage skips the query parser
questions.answer: Only the revenue and year columns need to be read — irrelevant columns (customer_name, address, etc.) are skipped entirely
questions.explanation: Row storage stores all columns together — to read revenue you must read the full row including all other columns. Column storage stores each column separately — reading SUM(revenue) reads only the revenue column. For a 100-column table, this is ~100x less I/O for a single-column aggregation.

questions.prompt: A heavy analytics query takes 4 minutes and is run by the finance team once a day at 9am. What is the correct architecture?
options: Run it on a read replica or data warehouse — not on the primary OLTP database
Add more indexes to the OLTP table
Run it at 3am when traffic is low on the primary
questions.answer: Run it on a read replica or data warehouse — not on the primary OLTP database
questions.explanation: A 4-minute query on the primary holds CPU/IO resources that the API needs for sub-millisecond transactions. Route analytics to a replica or a separate warehouse. The replica can absorb the 4-minute scan without impacting the live API.

questions.prompt: A startup has a single PostgreSQL database serving both the live API and the analytics dashboard. When should they separate them?
options: When analytics queries start visibly impacting API latency — 95th percentile API response time increases when the report runs
Immediately — always separate from day one
Never — PostgreSQL handles both workloads fine
Only if data exceeds 1 billion rows
questions.answer: When analytics queries start visibly impacting API latency — 95th percentile API response time increases when the report runs
questions.explanation: Premature separation adds operational complexity. A single PostgreSQL database is fine at small scale. Separate OLAP from OLTP when you observe measurable interference — analytics queries degrading API performance is the concrete signal.
